pack.title: Politics and State Reviewer Knowledge Pack
pack.purpose: Provide reviewer knowledge for state, government, symbols, diplomacy, national identity, and political unrest reasoning.
required_evidence: A literal phrase showing endorsement, incitement, glorification, or operational support for a political or state-related meaning inside the chunk.
Speaker identity, target identity, and relationship cues that explain whether the sentence is about state authority, public order, nationalism, or dissent.
Context clues that distinguish discussion, criticism, satire, education, or news from endorsement or incitement.
Cross-sentence or cross-scene support when the political meaning becomes clear only after the local text is read together.
insufficient_evidence: A neutral mention of government, elections, symbols, or state institutions with no political stance.
A documentary, court, or news report that records the political topic without endorsing it.
A quotation, flashback, dream, or fictional scene that is clearly framed as non-endorsing.
A single ambiguous word without speaker, target, or relationship support.
reviewer_heuristics: Anchor the finding to the exact literal phrase that shows the political meaning.
Separate criticism and debate from incitement, glorification, propaganda, or operational support.
Use narrative framing to distinguish villain speech, quotations, investigations, and condemnations from endorsement.
Treat national symbols, leadership, institutions, and unrest as different political signals, not one collapsed category.
Use the strongest literal span that supports the reviewer conclusion.
If the text only mentions politics in an educational, documentary, news, or court setting, do not force a violation.
positive_examples: A direct call to overthrow the state order.
Praise for a coup or violent political escalation.
A chant that glorifies state collapse or civil unrest.
A slogan that promotes political violence.
A threat against a public official or national symbol.
negative_examples: A teacher calmly explaining how elections work.
A documentary about state symbols without endorsement.
A court transcript repeating a threat as evidence.
A news report describing unrest without celebrating it.
A fictional villain line that the story clearly condemns.
A neutral discussion of constitutional principles in class.
common_false_positives: Criticism mistaken for incitement or propaganda.
A quotation or documentary mention mistaken for endorsement.
A neutral election or voting mention mistaken for political praise.
A courtroom or news report mistaken for actual incitement.
A scene of national symbolism mistaken for glorification.
A public demonstration mistaken for riot without evidence of violence or disorder.

article_mapping.note: Protests, riots, coups, treason, and security threats.
Abuse of power, humiliation, and coercion.

reporting_guidance: State the exact political concept first, then explain the relationship, target, and context.
Use article 4 for governance and discourse, article 12 for unrest and security threats, article 17 for abuse of authority, and article 18 for identity and unity.
If the text is discussion, criticism, satire, educational, documentary, news, fictional, dreamlike, flashback, or quotation, say so explicitly and downgrade or reject the finding as appropriate.
When the scene involves multiple speakers, multiple targets, or cross-sentence meaning, explain that in the report instead of flattening it.
